content:
Facebook rebranded as Meta last month, and the internet has responded with the energy it reserves for its favourite targets. Mockery, memes, the comfortable satisfaction of watching a powerful entity make what looks like a mistake. Zuckerberg's avatar, with its dead eyes and uncanny grin, has become the emblem of a pivot most commentators read as a desperate distraction from the company's mounting problems.

I'm not laughing, and it has nothing to do with thinking Meta will succeed. They might. They might not. The specific company matters far less than what the company is attempting, and what it's attempting is going to happen whether or not Meta is the one who does it.

The thesis is straightforward: persistent, immersive, shared virtual worlds are coming, and they're coming as infrastructure. As a platform layer sitting on top of the internet the way the internet sits on top of the physical network, becoming over time the primary environment in which a meaningful share of human activity occurs.

I can hear the objections already. The hardware is clunky. The experiences are thin. The avatars look like corporate clip art. The latency is nauseating, literally. Nobody wants a headset on for eight hours. The technology isn't ready.

All of that is true, and I don't think any of it matters.

Google Glass was true in exactly the same ways. Awkward hardware, wrong social dynamics, terrible battery life, and by any reasonable assessment a failure. Every single thing Glass tried to do - overlay digital information on the physical world, keep you connected without staring at a phone, put ambient computing at the edge of your visual field - is now done by a device everyone carries and nobody thinks twice about. Glass was right about the future and wrong about the present, and being early was indistinguishable from being wrong right up until the technology matured and the form factor changed.

The trajectory from text to images to video to real-time 3D environments is a direction of travel with decades of consistent momentum behind it, and nobody has to guess at it. Compute keeps getting cheaper on a curve showing no sign of flattening. Displays are improving in resolution, field of view and weight simultaneously. Tracking is getting more precise, haptics are developing, and each component of immersive experience is advancing on its own curve. The convergence of those curves points somewhere specific.

It points to the Oasis - Cline's term for the persistent virtual world everyone inhabits. I know how that sounds, and it's the kind of breathless futurism I normally distrust. But the Oasis is what you get by extending the current curves forward ten or fifteen years. Not fifty. Not a century. A decade and a half, possibly less.

**The Pioneer's Curse**

Zuckerberg sees the destination and I think he's probably right about it. What I'm much less sure about is whether he's building the right vehicle to reach it.

There's a pattern in technology I find instructive. The company that identifies a transformative platform shift often isn't the company that wins it. The pioneer builds something that proves the concept, establishes the category and demonstrates that demand exists, and then gets displaced by a competitor who learned from the pioneer's mistakes and executed better.

MySpace proved people wanted social networking. Facebook learned from MySpace and built something better. Friendster came before both. The graveyard of this industry is full of companies that were right about the future and wrong about the execution.

Zuckerberg knows this better than almost anyone, since he displaced Tom Anderson personally. He may be about to learn the lesson from the other side - spending tens of billions building the infrastructure, training the market, establishing the concept, and then watching someone else ship the version that works. The irony would be almost literary.

I've no idea who that someone will be. It could be a company that doesn't exist yet. It could be Apple, whose hardware instincts are better than Meta's. It could be an open-source collective, or a game studio, or something emerging from the intersection of AI and real-time rendering that nobody has anticipated.

**The Questions That Actually Matter**

What I'm confident about is that the Oasis is coming, whoever builds it. And the questions that matter are all about governance rather than technology, and we're currently asking none of them.

Who owns it? When a significant share of human social, economic and creative activity happens inside a virtual environment, the entity controlling that environment controls something more valuable than any physical real estate on earth. Not land. Experiential space. The environment in which human attention increasingly resides.

What are the rules? In a physical society, rules emerge from centuries of negotiation between the governed and the governing - constitutions, laws, rights, the accumulated infrastructure of civilised coexistence. In a virtual world the rules are written by a developer. The physics is programmed. The economy is designed. The rights of the inhabitants are whatever the creator decides they are, and they can change on a Tuesday.

Who has standing? If you build a life inside a virtual world - a business, a community, a creative practice, relationships - and the platform changes the rules, what recourse exists? In the physical world you have courts and constitutions and the hard-won protections of centuries of political evolution. In a virtual world you have the terms of service.

The measure I'd want established now, while none of this is settled, is a portability right: anything you create or accumulate inside one of these worlds - identity, assets, social graph, creative work - must be exportable in an open format, and the obligation should attach before any platform reaches scale rather than after.

I'd push for that ahead of any rule about conduct or content, because portability is what makes every other protection enforceable. A world you cannot leave is a world whose operator has no reason to treat you well. A world you can leave has to earn you. We learned this lesson with telephone numbers and bank accounts and we learned it late both times, after the incumbents were entrenched enough to fight it for a decade. The Oasis doesn't exist yet, which makes this the only moment when the rule costs nobody anything to accept.

Everyone is mocking the metaverse, and I think they're mocking a first draft. The final version will be extraordinary, it won't be optional, and the company that builds it may well not be the one that renamed itself after the concept.

The Oasis is coming. The question is who builds it, who owns it, and whether we think about governance before it arrives or afterwards. History suggests afterwards, which means too late - and the only thing that has ever changed that pattern is somebody raising it while the whole thing still looks faintly ridiculous.
